title: Kindness and bias
hookLine: a few weeks of loving-kindness practice reduced one measure of racial bias in one study (Kang, Gray and Dovidio)

cards: Some reactions arrive before any thought does. A face on a train, a voice on the phone, an accent at the counter, and something in the body leans in or leans away a split second before the mind has a say.
Psychologists have built tests to catch those split seconds, and what they catch can be uncomfortable: quiet leanings people would never choose and might never admit.
If compassion can be trained, can a practice of goodwill reach down into those split seconds too?

teach.b: First, the practice, which this path met on day two hundred forty-two. Loving-kindness, in Pali metta, comes from Buddhist teaching.

A short discourse called the Metta Sutta describes it: wishing that all beings be happy and at ease, weak or strong, near or far, seen or unseen, and holding that goodwill toward the whole world the way a mother guards her only child.
Psychologists Yoona Kang, Jeremy Gray and John Dovidio gave a group of non-Black adults a short course in loving-kindness practice over a few weeks.
A second group learned about loving-kindness and discussed it, but didn't practice it. A third group simply waited. Third, the measure.
Afterward, everyone took a timed computer test of automatic associations, the kind that catches split-second leanings.
The group that actually practiced showed less automatic bias toward Black people, and toward homeless people too. The group that only talked about it did not. Fourth, the size of it.
This was one study, one kind of test, a modest group of people. Those tests are debated among psychologists, and nobody showed that a few weeks of practice rewrote anyone's whole outlook.
So the careful claim is small: in this study, information alone didn't move the measure. Practice did: wishing well, again and again, toward a circle that keeps getting wider.

how: In Buddhist loving-kindness (metta) practice, people repeat simple wishes for well-being, starting with themselves or a loved one and widening step by step to strangers, difficult people and all beings, as the Metta Sutta describes.

games.q: you're in the study. you can practice loving-kindness, discuss it in a group, or wait. which one moved the bias measure?
games.why: only the practice group showed less automatic bias. information alone didn't do it; practice did.

practice: Hold one simple wish for someone you love: may you be happy, may you be at ease.

Then bring to mind someone who seems very unlike you, in age, background or how they live, a face from the bus, the checkout line or the news, and offer them the same wish, with the same warmth, as if they were just as near.
